title: David Fowler (Montaukett)
summary: David Fowler (1735–1807) was a Montaukett teacher, traveler, community organizer, and political leader whose work connected Montauk to the Native-led Brothertown movement.
content:
David Fowler (1735–1807) was a Montaukett teacher, traveler, community organizer, and political leader whose work connected Montauk with Native communities in Connecticut and central New York. He was a brother-in-law and close associate of the Mohegan minister Samson Occom, but the surviving record shows Fowler as an important organizer in his own right. He taught in Native schools, carried messages and supplies across long distances, helped develop the Brothertown plan, and later served in Brothertown community government.1

Montaukett family and education

Sources identify Fowler as Montaukett and place his birth at Montauk in 1735. Family histories name James Fowler, a Shinnecock man, and Betty Pharaoh Fowler, a Montaukett woman, as his parents. His sister Mary Fowler married Samson Occom, creating the family relationship that appears often in later accounts. On April 12, 1759, at age twenty-four, David entered Eleazar Wheelock’s Moor’s Indian Charity School in Lebanon, Connecticut. Wheelock’s school was part of a colonial missionary system, but Native students also used literacy, travel, and education to pursue community goals that exceeded the institution’s plans for them.2

Teacher and traveler

In 1761 Fowler accompanied Occom into Oneida country. That work helped him build relationships in the region where the Brothertown community would later be established. In 1765 he became a schoolmaster at Canajoharie. The record does not present his teaching as uncomplicated: John A. Strong preserves criticism that Fowler punished students severely, while other accounts emphasize his endurance and service. Including both parts of the record avoids turning a complex Native teacher into either a missionary ideal or a simple hero.3

During a famine in 1767, Fowler made a demanding relief journey from Canajoharie through New England to obtain supplies. Stone’s account says he covered about 400 miles in ten days. Later that year, David, his wife Hannah, and their young son returned to Montauk, where he taught and helped care for his parents. When his parents’ wigwam burned in 1770, family survival took priority and the mission school appointed another teacher.4

Building Brothertown

The Brothertown plan took shape in 1773 as Native families from Long Island and southern New England sought land where they could live together under growing colonial pressure. Fowler and Occom were central organizers. In March 1775, Fowler led an early group of Montaukett people from Long Island to the new settlement in Oneida country. The move was not an abandonment of Montaukett identity; it was a Native-led response to dispossession, missionary pressure, and the need to protect community life.5

The Revolutionary War displaced the new community, and many Brothertown families temporarily took refuge near Stockbridge. Fowler later returned to central New York and helped rebuild. Sources distinguish Occom’s spiritual leadership from Fowler’s political and practical work, describing Fowler as a senior peacemaker and trustee. In 1787 his mother, Betty Pharaoh Fowler, moved from Long Island to live with him. Fowler also opposed efforts to lease Brothertown land to white settlers. He died in 1807 after more than three decades of organizing, resettlement, and community leadership.6

Distinguishing people with the same name

Later Montaukett records include more than one person named David Fowler. A caption in The History and Archaeology of the Montauk identifies a photographed grave as belonging to “the missionary David Fowler” and also calls him a brother of Maria Pharaoh. That relationship cannot describe the eighteenth-century David Fowler documented as living from 1735 to 1807. This biography therefore treats the caption as a later-name conflation and does not attach Maria Pharaoh to his immediate family.7

Reading the map

The numbered map points show a dated chronology using broad, public locations: Montauk, Lebanon, Oneida country, Canajoharie, a return to Montauk, and Brothertown. The connecting line is not a reconstruction of Fowler’s exact route and should not be read as one.

  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), pp. 160, 162, 164, 172, 186, 536, and 539.
  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. 71–72.
  • Long Island Forum, vol. IX, no. 3, p. 27.
  • David Bunn Martine, Shinnecock History Timeline, pp. 7–8.
why_this_matters: David Fowler’s life shows Montaukett history extending far beyond one place. His teaching, long-distance service, family responsibilities, and Brothertown leadership reveal Native people using education, kinship, movement, and government to sustain community under colonial land pressure.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Montaukett organizer David Fowler with a six-stop life chronology, six linked Historic Moments, and an identity note separating him from a later namesake.
